# Occupied-parity weighted centers with a strict minimal-face mass

This is a complete finite lattice theorem. It does not prove OC for
general mixed-integer convex bodies. In particular, its weights and
centers are on the integer base, and it makes no assertion that a
nonaffine graph of fiber centroids preserves base halfspaces.

## 1. Definitions and theorem

Let A be a finite-dimensional real affine space, and let Lambda be an
affine lattice in A. Thus Lambda=c+L, where L is a discrete additive
subgroup spanning the direction space of A. The rank-zero lattice is
allowed. The parity classes of Lambda are its cosets modulo 2L; this
notion does not depend on the chosen origin c in Lambda.

Let P be a nonempty finite set satisfying

    P=conv(P) intersect Lambda.

Write Q=conv(P), let k be the number of parity classes occupied by P,
and assign each p in P a positive real weight w_p. Put

    M=sum_{p in P} w_p,       alpha=M/k.

For p in P define its unnormalized weighted halfspace depth by

    delta_w(p)=min { sum_{q in P intersect H} w_q :
                    H is a closed affine halfspace containing p }.

When A has dimension zero the entire space is the sole permitted
halfspace trace. In positive dimension, allowing the entire space as
an additional trace has no effect. Define

    D(w)={p in P : delta_w(p)>=alpha}.

The minimal face F_p is the unique face of the polytope Q whose
relative interior contains p. The polytope Q itself counts as a face.
The notation w(F) means sum_{p in P intersect F}w_p.

**Theorem.** The set D(w) is nonempty. Moreover there is a point

    p in D(w) with w(F_p)>M/k                         (1)

unless P consists of exactly k vertices of Q and all k weights equal
M/k. In this exceptional case every p in P has depth M/k and minimal
face mass M/k, so (1) is impossible.

In particular (1) always holds when |P|>k. There is no restriction on
the dimension, rank, shape, rationality of weights, or orientations
of the halfspaces.

We prove every discrete and separation step below. Only elementary
finite-dimensional strict separation and the finite halfspace
description of a polytope are used as ordinary convex facts.

## 2. Finite occupied-parity Helly lemma

**Lemma 1.** Suppose a finite family of closed affine linear
inequalities has no common solution in P. Then at most k inequalities
from that family already have no common solution in P.

**Proof.** Write the inequalities as a_i(x)<=b_i, for 1<=i<=s,
where the a_i are affine linear functions. For each p in P at least
one inequality is violated. Finiteness gives

    eta_0=min_{p in P} max_i(a_i(p)-b_i)>0.

Choose 0<eta<eta_0 and set beta_i=b_i+eta. The strict system
a_i(x)<beta_i still has no solution in P. Choose

    T_i>max(beta_i, max_{p in P} a_i(p)).

Let B be the following set of threshold vectors c in R^s:

    beta_i<=c_i<=T_i for every i,
    for every p in P there is an i with a_i(p)>=c_i.

It is a nonempty compact set: beta belongs to it, and its defining
conditions are a finite intersection of finite unions of closed
conditions within a bounded box. Choose c in B maximizing sum_i c_i.
Call i nonsaturated if c_i<T_i.

For every nonsaturated i there is a point p_i in P with

    a_i(p_i)=c_i,       a_j(p_i)<c_j for every j!=i.   (2)

Indeed consider only those p for which a_j(p)<c_j for all j!=i.
Since c belongs to B, each such p has a_i(p)>=c_i. If equality
never holds, all these inequalities are strict, and their positive
gaps have a positive minimum because P is finite. Increasing c_i by
less than that minimum and less than T_i-c_i preserves membership in
B, contradicting maximality. If there are no such p, any sufficiently
small increase works and gives the same contradiction.

The points p_i in (2) are distinct. If i!=j and p_i,p_j had the same
parity, their midpoint m would belong to Lambda. It belongs to Q by
convexity and therefore belongs to P. At inequality i one endpoint
has equality and the other strict inequality; the same holds at j.
At every other inequality both endpoints have strict inequality.
Consequently a_l(m)<c_l for every l, contradicting c in B. There are
therefore at most k nonsaturated indices.

Every saturated inequality a_i(x)<T_i is strictly satisfied by all
points of P. Hence the nonsaturated inequalities alone exclude P
from the strict system a_i(x)<c_i. Their original closed inequalities
a_i(x)<=b_i are stronger, since b_i<beta_i<=c_i. Thus those at most
k original inequalities also have no common solution in P. QED.

**Lemma 2.** Let K_1,...,K_s be polytopes in A. If their intersection
contains no point of P, then some at most k of them already have an
intersection containing no point of P.

**Proof.** An empty K_i proves the claim immediately. Otherwise give
each K_i a finite closed halfspace description in A, using paired
inequalities for affine-hull equations when needed. Apply Lemma 1 to
the combined finite system. Assign each selected inequality to its
original polytope. There are at most k such polytopes; their common
intersection is contained in the selected inequalities and therefore
misses P. QED.

## 3. Weighted center existence, with boundary atoms retained

**Lemma 3.** D(w) is nonempty.

**Proof.** Consider the finite family

    K_E=conv(E),     E subset P with w(E)>M-alpha.

Each such E is nonempty. Any s<=k of these subsets have a common
point of P: their complements have total weight strictly less than
s alpha<=M, so their union cannot cover P. The corresponding s
polytopes thus have a common point of P. Lemma 2 shows that all K_E
have a common point p in P.

If a closed halfspace H containing p had w(P intersect H)<alpha,
then E=P\H would satisfy w(E)>M-alpha. All points of this finite E
lie strictly on the complementary side of the defining hyperplane,
as does their convex hull. This contradicts p in conv(E) and p in H.
Hence delta_w(p)>=alpha. No mass on the boundary of H has been
discarded. QED.

The possible halfspace traces P intersect H form a finite family of
subsets of P. Thus every depth in the definition is an attained
minimum of a finite set of weight sums. In particular, for any two
weight vectors w,w' on P,

    |delta_w(p)-delta_w'(p)|<=sum_{q in P}|w_q-w'_q|.  (3)

Every proper face F of Q is exposed. A closed supporting halfspace
therefore has trace exactly P intersect F. This also gives, with
the trivial total-mass bound when F_p=Q,

    delta_w(p)<=w(F_p).                              (4)

## 4. The only balanced cover by faces of mass alpha

If k=1, P is a singleton. For otherwise choose a closest pair of
distinct points in P in any Euclidean norm on A. They have the same
parity, so their midpoint belongs to P and is a closer distinct point,
a contradiction. Thus k=1 is already the exceptional case. Assume
k>=2 for the rest of the proof, so alpha<M.

Let F be the finite family of faces of Q having weight exactly alpha.
All these faces are proper and nonempty. Write chi_F in {0,1}^P for
their incidence vectors.

**Lemma 4.** Exactly one of the following alternatives holds:

    (a) There is v in R^P with sum_p v_p=0 and
        sum_{p in F}v_p<0 for every F in F.

    (b) P consists of exactly k vertices of Q and all weights are alpha.

If F is empty, (a) is interpreted vacuously and holds with v=0.

**Proof.** Suppose F is nonempty and (a) fails. Put

    x0=(1/k) 1_P.

We claim x0 lies in the convex hull of the finitely many chi_F.
If not, strict separation supplies v with v dot chi_F<v dot x0
for every F. Replace v by

    v'=v-(sum_p v_p/M) w,

where w denotes the vector of the weights. Then sum_p v'_p=0, and
because w dot chi_F=alpha=M/k,

    v' dot chi_F=v dot chi_F-(sum_p v_p)/k<0.

This is (a), a contradiction. Therefore there are coefficients
lambda_F>=0 such that

    sum_F lambda_F chi_F=1_P,       sum_F lambda_F=k. (5)

Discard zero coefficients, and partition P according to its incidence
vector in the remaining faces. If p,q have the same parity, then
m=(p+q)/2 belongs to P. For every face F,

    chi_F(m)=chi_F(p)chi_F(q).                       (6)

This is the defining face property: an interior point of a segment
in Q belongs to F exactly when both endpoints belong to F. The
nonnegative quantities chi_F(p)+chi_F(q)-2chi_F(m), multiplied by
lambda_F and summed, give 1+1-2=0 by (5). Consequently for every
positive-coefficient face their three incidences agree. In particular
all points in one parity class lie in one incidence class, and the
midpoint of any same-parity pair belongs to their incidence class.

Let l be the number of incidence classes. The first assertion gives
l<=k. By coverage in (5), each incidence class is contained in some
positive-coefficient face, and thus has weight at most alpha. Since
the weights of these classes sum to M=k alpha, we also have l>=k.
It follows that l=k, every class has weight alpha, and each class
consists of exactly one occupied parity class: the map from the k
parities onto the k incidence classes is a bijection.

Each incidence class is therefore a finite set of one parity closed
under taking pairwise midpoints. The closest-pair argument above
forces each class to be a singleton. Thus P has exactly k points,
each of weight alpha. Every positive-coefficient face has weight
alpha, so it contains exactly one such point. Equation (5) covers
every point, hence every point lies in a singleton face and is a
vertex. This proves (b).

Conversely, in (b) all singleton vertex faces have weight alpha.
A zero-sum vector cannot be strictly negative on every singleton.
Thus (a) fails. This proves the exclusive alternatives. QED.

The midpoint-closure assertion used above refers to the incidence
class of a same-parity pair. Before l=k is known, one must not assume
that an entire incidence class consists of a single parity; the
bijection argument establishes precisely that missing fact.

## 5. One perturbation selects a strict-face center

Assume we are not in the exceptional case. Choose v from Lemma 4.
If v=0 because there are no faces of mass alpha, any point in D(w)
works by (4). Otherwise define

    w^epsilon=w+epsilon v.

Choose a single sufficiently small epsilon>0 as follows. Positivity
of the original finite weight vector ensures all new weights remain
positive. Their total is exactly M. For every old noncenter p not
in D(w), the gap alpha-delta_w(p) is positive. Finitely many such
gaps and (3) allow us to choose epsilon so that

    delta_w^epsilon(p)<alpha for every p not in D(w). (7)

For every face G whose old mass is strictly below alpha, choose
epsilon still smaller if necessary so that w^epsilon(G)<alpha.
There are finitely many faces. For every face with old mass exactly
alpha, the strict inequalities of Lemma 4 give w^epsilon(G)<alpha
for every positive epsilon. Consequently

    w(G)<=alpha implies w^epsilon(G)<alpha           (8)

for every face G of Q. (The full face Q never meets the premise.)

Apply Lemma 3 to the positive weights w^epsilon. It gives a single
point p in P with delta_w^epsilon(p)>=alpha. By (7), this point
also belongs to D(w). By (4) for the perturbed weights,
w^epsilon(F_p)>=alpha. Equation (8) now forces w(F_p)>alpha,
which proves (1). There is no limiting sequence or moving lattice
point in this argument; epsilon is fixed once, and any one of its
finitely many centers can be selected. An arbitrary fixed ordering
of P can make the selection deterministic by taking the first.

In the exceptional case all points are vertices of weight alpha.
Every halfspace containing p includes its own atom, so depth is at
least alpha. The supporting halfspace exposing p has precisely that
atom, so depth equals alpha. Its minimal face is {p}, also of mass
alpha. Thus no strict-face center exists, completing the theorem.

## 6. Scope, equality, and affine lattices

The proof uses only midpoint closure of conv(P) intersect Lambda,
finite convex separation, finite cap traces, and positive weights.
Every affine isomorphism carrying one affine lattice onto another
preserves these ingredients and the number of occupied classes
modulo twice the lattice. No Euclidean measure, determinant factor,
integer dimension bound, or coordinate normalization enters.

The failure characterization is exact: it requires simultaneously
one point per occupied parity, convex position, and equal weights.
When |P|=k but some weight exceeds alpha, its atom alone guarantees
depth and minimal-face mass strictly larger than alpha. When all
weights equal alpha but a point is not a vertex, that point is a
center by its own atom and its minimal face contains other atoms.
These observations also directly confirm the two nonexceptional
possibilities at |P|=k.

For an ambient integer lattice of dimension n this gives the sharper
occupied-parity threshold M/k, with k<=2^n. It does not by itself
give the mixed-integer OC constant for nonlinear centroid graphs or
arbitrary convex fibers.

## 7. A scoped midpoint-label extension

The same theorem holds in the following more general finite setting.
Let P be a nonempty finite subset of an arbitrary real affine space,
and give its points k occupied labels. Assume that whenever distinct
p,q have the same label, their actual geometric midpoint (p+q)/2
belongs to P. The midpoint is not assumed in advance to have the
same label. Define weights, depths, and minimal faces as above.
Then there is a center with minimal-face mass strictly greater than
M/k, except exactly when P consists of k equally weighted vertices.

Indeed Lemma 1 uses the lattice hypothesis only to place the midpoint
of two same-label witnesses in P. Lemmas 2 and 3 are unchanged. In
Lemma 4 the labels map onto the incidence classes; equality of their
numbers makes this map a bijection. Only then does (6) show that the
midpoint has the same label as its two endpoints. The closest-pair
argument is therefore justified exactly as before. If k=1, the sole
label already makes all pairwise midpoints belong to P and forces a
singleton. All remaining steps use only finite traces and faces.

In particular this extension applies to a finite lifted graph

    Ptilde={(p,g_p):p in P0}

with labels given by the parities of the base points, provided that
EVERY same-parity pair p,q has midpoint m=(p+q)/2 in P0 and satisfies

    g_m=(g_p+g_q)/2.

This condition concerns all such pairs. Tightness on only a selected
collection of midpoint comparisons does not establish it. The
extension asserts a finite weighted halfspace-center theorem in the
lifted space; it does not supply the missing midpoint identities for
a general mixed-integer convex body.
